procedural_history.impugned_order: Order dated March 25, 1964, terminating the appellant's service under Rule 12 of the M.P. Government Servants (Temporary and Quasi-permanent Service) Rules, 1960.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The appellant filed a writ petition (Misc. Petition No. 272 of 1964) in the Madhya Pradesh High Court to quash the order dated March 25, 1964. The High Court summarily dismissed the petition, holding that the order was not by way of punishment and that the appellant's services were liable to be terminated under Rule 12 on one month's notice. The point that the High Court had recommended the appellant's confirmation was not raised in the High Court.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant appealed to the Supreme Court after obtaining special leave. The appellant contended that r. 12 was violative of Arts. 14 and 16 of the Constitution u it oonferrcd arbitrary and unguided discretion to the Government~ (ii) tlae impugned order was irivalid as it was passed without consulting the State Public Service Commission under Art. 320(3)(c) of the Comtilution; (iii) the order was passed by way of punishment without givinji ~ appellant an oppoounity to show cause against the prC'pOSCd action and wu therefore violaltve of Art. 311 of the Constitution; (iv) tbe order was In violation of the principles of natural justice, as no charge-sheet wu SCl'Ved nor any departmental inquiry beld; and (v) the State Government ctrcd Ui blindly following the recommendations of the High Court. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, finding that the order did not cast any stigma on the appellant's character or integrity, was not passed by way of punishment, and did not deprive the appellant of any vested right.

issue.issue_text: Whether Rule 12 was unconstitutional as it was framed without consulting the State Public Service Commission and the High Court.

facts: The appellant's counsel argued that Rule 12 was unconstitutional.
The basis for this argument was that the rule was allegedly framed without consulting the State Public Service Commission and the High Court.
law: The Supreme Court characterized this contention as raising "mixed questions of law and fact."

There is a procedural principle that new arguments, particularly those involving facts, cannot be raised for the first time in an appeal to the Supreme Court if they were not raised in the lower court (the High Court).
application: The Court noted that this specific argument—that the rule was unconstitutional for lack of consultation—was not raised by the appellant in the High Court.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument and refused to consider its merits because it was a new issue being raised for the first time on appeal.

issue.issue_text: Whether the termination order cast a stigma on the appellant's character or was passed by way of punishment, thereby attracting the provisions of Article 311 of the Constitution.

facts: The appellant was a temporary government servant in the judicial service.
Complaints were made against the appellant regarding his association with a girl and taking bribes.
The High Court conducted an inquiry into these complaints and recommended the termination of the appellant's service.
The State Government then issued a termination order under Rule 12 of the M. P. Government Servants (Temporary and Quasi-permanent Service) Rules, 1960.
The termination order itself simply stated that the appellant's services were terminated and did not mention the complaints or the inquiry.
law: Article 311 of the Constitution provides protections to civil servants when an action is taken by way of punishment.
A temporary government servant has no right to hold the office, and their services can be terminated under the applicable service rules (in this case, Rule 12).

A termination order that is 'unexceptionable in form' and is preceded by an inquiry launched only to ascertain whether the public servant should be retained in service does not attract the provisions of Article 311.
application: The Court first examined the termination order itself and found that, 'on the face of it,' the order did not cast any stigma on the appellant's character or integrity.

The Court determined that the inquiry that preceded the termination was not a formal disciplinary proceeding but an informal inquiry to ascertain the appellant's suitability to be retained in service.
As the appellant was a temporary government servant, he had no vested right to the office, and the government had the right to terminate his services under Rule 12.
Because the order itself was non-stigmatic and the preceding inquiry was only for determining suitability, the Court concluded that the termination was not a punishment.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the termination order was not passed by way of punishment and did not cast a stigma on the appellant's character. It was a simple termination of a temporary employee's service as permitted by the rules. Therefore, the protections of Article 311 of the Constitution were not attracted.

issue.issue_text: Whether the appellant's services could be terminated on one month's notice, given that his confirmation was allegedly recommended and the job advertisement did not specify this condition.

facts: The appellant, a temporary civil judge, argued that his services could not be terminated on one month's notice.

He based this argument on two points: (a) the High Court had allegedly recommended his confirmation, and (b) the job advertisement he responded to did not mention that his services could be terminated on one month's notice.
law: A legal point or argument that was not raised in a lower court (the High Court, in this case) cannot be raised for the first time before the Supreme Court.
The employment of a government servant is subject to the relevant service rules.
Under Rule 12 of the M. P. Government Servants (Temporary and Quasi-permanent Service) Rules, 1960, the services of a temporary government servant could be terminated on one month's notice.
application: The Court refused to consider the argument about the recommended confirmation because the appellant had not raised this point in the High Court, and therefore could not raise it for the first time in the Supreme Court.
The Court found it "immaterial" that the job advertisement did not mention the termination clause.

The Court reasoned that the appellant's services were governed by the applicable service rules, specifically Rule 12, which allowed for termination on one month's notice. His status as a temporary government servant meant he was subject to these rules regardless of the advertisement's content.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellant's arguments, holding that the point about confirmation could not be raised for the first time, and the terms of the job advertisement were irrelevant because the governing service rules (Rule 12) explicitly allowed for the termination of a temporary servant's services on one month's notice.

issue.issue_text: Whether the appellant was a temporary government servant whose services could be terminated on one month's notice under Rule 12.

facts: The appellant was appointed as a temporary Civil Judge in Madhya Pradesh.
The appellant was not in quasi-permanent service.
There was no provision in the appellant's order of appointment or in any agreement stating that his service could not be terminated on one month's notice.
law: Rule 12 of the Madhya Pradesh Government Servants (Temporary and Quasi-permanent Service) Rules, 1960, provides that the service of a temporary government servant who is not in quasi-permanent service is liable to termination at any time by one month's notice.
application: The Court determined that the appellant's employment status was that of a temporary government servant, and therefore, his service was subject to the relevant rules, including Rule 12.
The Court rejected the appellant's argument that the job advertisement's failure to mention the possibility of termination was relevant, deeming it "immaterial."

The Court also refused to consider the appellant's point that the High Court had recommended his confirmation, as this argument was not raised in the lower court and could not be raised for the first time before the Supreme Court.
As a temporary servant, the appellant had no vested right to hold the office, and the state government had the right to terminate his services under Rule 12.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court held that the appellant was a temporary government servant, not in quasi-permanent service, and his services could be legally terminated on one month's notice under Rule 12.

respondent_arguments: This issue could not be raised for the first time in the Supreme Court as it was not raised in the High Court and involves mixed questions of law and fact.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the termination order cast a stigma on the appellant's character or was passed by way of punishment, thereby attracting the provisions of Article 311 of the Constitution.
appellant_arguments: The termination order was punitive and violated Article 311 of the Constitution because it was passed without giving the appellant an opportunity to show cause.
The real reason for termination, as indicated by the respondent's own statement about complaints regarding the appellant's association with a young woman, made the order stigmatic.
respondent_arguments: The termination order, on its face, did not cast any stigma on the appellant's character or integrity.
The order did not visit the appellant with any evil consequences and was not passed by way of punishment, so the provisions of Article 311 were not attracted.

The job advertisement for the temporary post did not specify that services could be terminated on one month's notice.
respondent_arguments: The point about the High Court's recommendation for confirmation was not raised in the lower court and cannot be raised for the first time here.
It is immaterial that the advertisement did not mention the termination condition, as the appellant's services were subject to the relevant rules, including Rule 12.

cases.case_name: State of U.P. v. M. L. Srivastava
cases.principle: The provisions of Art. 320(3)(c) of the Constitution are not mandatory and do not confer any rights on the public servant, and the absence of consultation with the State Public Service Commission does not afford him a cause of action.

cases.case_name: State of Punjab v. Sukh Raj Bahadur
cases.principle: An order of termination of service in unexceptionable form preceded by an enquiry launched by the superior authorities only to ascertain whether the public servant should be retained in service, does not attract the operation of Article 311 of the Constitution.

cases.case_name: State of West Bengal v. N. N. Bagchi
cases.principle: This case was followed to repel the contention that the State Government acted improperly by following the recommendations of the High Court regarding the termination of a judicial officer's service.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The government can properly terminate the services of a temporary subordinate judicial officer, who has no right to hold the office, based on the recommendation of the High Court, which is vested with control over the subordinate judiciary. Such a termination under the relevant service rules does not attract the provisions of Article 311 of the Constitution, provided the order does not cast a stigma or is not passed by way of punishment.
obiter: A legal challenge to a service rule that raises mixed questions of law and fact cannot be raised for the first time in the Supreme Court.
It is immaterial that a job advertisement for a temporary post did not specifically mention that services could be terminated under the applicable rules.
A factual point not raised in the High Court cannot be allowed to be raised for the first time in the Supreme Court.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The appellant was a temporary government servant who had no right to hold the office. As such, the State government had the right to terminate his services under Rule 12 without issuing a notice to show cause. The termination order, on its face, did not cast any stigma on the appellant's character or integrity, nor did it visit him with any evil consequences. Therefore, it was not passed by way of punishment, and the provisions of Article 311 of the Constitution were not attracted.
legal_tests_applied: Whether a termination order, on its face, casts a stigma on the employee's character or integrity or visits them with evil consequences, which would indicate it is punitive and attract Article 311.
Whether an employee has a vested right to hold an office, the deprivation of which would require adherence to the principles of natural justice.
Whether a constitutional provision, such as Article 320(3)(c) regarding consultation with the Public Service Commission, is mandatory or directory in nature.
why_appellant_lost: The argument that Rule 12 was unconstitutional for lack of consultation could not be raised for the first time in the Supreme Court as it involved mixed questions of law and fact that were not raised in the High Court.

The termination order was not punitive or stigmatic because, 'On the face of it, the order did not cast any stigma on the appellant's character or integrity nor did it visit him with any evil consequences. It was not passed by way of punishment and the provisions of Art. 311 were not attrac!ed.'

The failure to consult the State Public Service Commission was not a valid ground for appeal, as the court affirmed that 'the provisions of Art. 320(3)(c) were not mandatory and did not confer any rights on the public servant and that the-absence of consultation with the State Public Service Commission · did not afforu him a cause of action.'

The principles of natural justice were not violated because, unlike cases where an employee has a right to the office, 'the impugned order did not depnve the appellant of any vested right. The appellant was a temporary government servant and had no ri&ltt to bold the office.'
why_respondent_won: The appellant's status as a temporary government servant was determinative: 'The appellant was a temporary government servant and had no right to hold the office.'

As a temporary servant, the government had the authority to terminate his employment under the rules: 'The State government had the right to terminate his services under rule 12 without issuing any notice to the appellant to show cause against the proposed action.'

The government acted properly by following the recommendation of the High Court, which has constitutional authority over the subordinate judiciary: 'The High Court is vested with the control over the subordinate judiciary... If the High Court found that the appellant was not a. lit person to be retained in service, it could properly ask the goverilinent to termi11ate bis services.'
policy_considerations: The High Court is vested with control over the subordinate judiciary, and it is proper for the government to act on the High Court's recommendation regarding the fitness of a judicial officer to be retained in service.

New arguments involving mixed questions of law and fact cannot be raised for the first time before the Supreme Court, reinforcing procedural propriety and the importance of raising all relevant issues at the High Court level.
